passages.t: Anyone left from the house of Saul
passages.happening:
With his kingdom secure, David asks, “Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” (verse 1).

A servant of Saul's family named Ziba is brought to him. David asks again, “Is there anyone left of Saul’s family to whom I can show the kindness of God?” Ziba answered, “There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet” (verse 3). He is living at Lo-debar, in the house of Machir son of Ammiel. David sends for him.

Mephibosheth comes and falls on his face. “Do not be afraid,” said David, “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table” (verse 7). Mephibosheth bows down: “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
David is keeping an old promise. Years before, while Saul hunted David, Jonathan had asked him to swear never to cut off his kindness from Jonathan's household (1 Samuel 20:14-17). Jonathan died on Mount Gilboa, and his son, then five, was lamed when his nurse fled with him at the news (4:4).

In that world a man who founded a new dynasty usually removed the surviving men of the old one, since any of them could become the center of a rival claim. So Mephibosheth had good reason to be living quietly east of the Jordan, at Lo-debar in Gilead, and good reason to fall on his face in fear when the king sent for him.

The chapter is built around one word, kindness, chesed in Hebrew, the loyal love that keeps faith with a covenant. David uses it three times (verses 1, 3 and 7). The kindness of God means kindness of the kind God shows, or kindness sworn before God. It reaches past Jonathan, to whom the promise was made, to a son who had done nothing to earn it.

A dead dog was the lowest thing a man could call himself. Dogs were scavengers in that world, not pets. A disabled man from a fallen house expected nothing, and the distance between his words and David's gift is the point of the scene.
passages.later: Israel's later history shows what new kings usually did. ‘As soon as Baasha became king, he struck down the entire household of Jeroboam’ (1 Kings 15:29), and Jehu wiped out the house of Ahab (2 Kings 10). David does the opposite.
passages.hard:
Was David's kindness real, or was he keeping a possible rival where he could watch him?

Some interpreters read the chapter with political suspicion. Mephibosheth was Saul's heir, and bringing him to Jerusalem kept him within reach. Some have also argued that the events of chapter 21, where David hands over seven of Saul's descendants to be put to death, came before this chapter, so that David's question in verse 1 is less innocent than it sounds.

Others take the narrator at his word. David is keeping an oath to Jonathan, and he gives back land he could easily have kept. Both things can be true at once, since in the ancient world generosity and good sense often walked together. The text itself frames the act as kindness for Jonathan's sake, and it later records that David spared Mephibosheth because of that oath (21:7).
passages.asks: David remembered a promise he had made when he was in danger and Jonathan was powerful. Ask what promises you made in a hard season that are easy to forget now. And ask who might be living quietly afraid of you, waiting to be sent for.

passages.t: A place at the king's table
passages.happening:
David calls Ziba and gives Mephibosheth all that had belonged to Saul and his house. Ziba, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, is to farm the land for him, ‘But Mephibosheth, your master’s grandson, is always to eat at my table’ (verse 10). Ziba agrees.

‘So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table like one of the king’s own sons’ (verse 11). He has a young son named Mica. The chapter ends: ‘So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table, and he was lame in both feet’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Eating at the king's table was a public honor and lifelong support. It could also keep a possible rival close. Saul's family land, probably around Gibeah in Benjamin, had likely passed to the crown or been managed by Ziba. David gives it back to its heir and makes Ziba's whole household responsible for working it.

The table is the chapter's central picture, mentioned four times: food, honor and belonging. To eat there was to be treated like one of the king's own sons. Disability could bring social shame in that world, as the saying about the blind and the lame in 5:8 shows. David's welcome goes against both Mephibosheth's fallen rank and his weakness.

The last line is left open on purpose. Mephibosheth always ate at the king's table, and he was lame in both feet. His weakness stays in view even as he sits among the king's sons. He is not healed first and welcomed after. He is welcomed as he is.

Ziba and Mephibosheth will both return in the days of Absalom's revolt (chapters 16 and 19), when every loyalty is tested.
passages.later:
The books of Kings end with a scene like this one. The king of Babylon released Judah's exiled king, Jehoiachin, from prison, ‘and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life’ (2 Kings 25:29).

A proverb names the spirit of David's act: “Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender” (Proverbs 19:17).
passages.asks: Mephibosheth was given a seat at the table without first being made strong. Ask whether you think you must fix your weakness before you can belong. And ask whom you could make room for at your own table, as they are.
